column4: The source's form رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ (“to be seen by people”) occurs here; charity for display is likened to dust on smooth stone washed bare, exposing an outward act without enduring substance.
يُرَاءُونَ النَّاسَ places people as the audience for prayer; the verse calls that prayer lazy, matching the section's visible worship whose reality is governed by who watches.
رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ describes spending for a human audience, the same source-root branch as people-facing display; this ayah's specific act is spending wealth.
رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ names display in this verse's departure scene, paired with turning from Allah's way; it shows the same root's public performance in another act.
The exact opening أَرَأَيْتَ redirects attention to the one forbidding prayer; as in the section, the question asks the listener to recognize a person's conduct, not report literal sight.
The next ayah names the servant praying, completing the scene of prayer being obstructed and supplying the visible act against which 107 sets people-facing worship.
The second أَرَأَيْتَ asks the Prophet to consider one who denies and turns away; the formula again summons judgment of character rather than surface looking.
ٱللَّهَ يَرَىٰ names the actual seer in this passage, completing the contrast between people's gaze sought by performers and divine sight.
Allah is named as the one who sees the Prophet when he stands; the verse places standing worship within the true audience's sight.
It extends that sight to تَقَلُّبَكَ فِي السَّاجِدِينَ, so the Prophet's movement among those prostrating is seen by Allah.
أَفَرَءَيْتَ ٱلَّذِي تَوَلَّىٰ uses the attention-directing question for one who turns away, then its own context exposes his giving and withholding.
وَأَعْطَىٰ قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدَىٰ says he gives little then stops; that concrete withholding echoes the section's small aid and completes the same see-and-judge scene.
When seen, their bodies impress, yet the verse compares them to propped-up timber; this visual contrast between pleasing exterior and inert appearance meets the section's mirror and demeanor image.
خَائِنَةَ الْأَعْيُنِ وَمَا تُخْفِي الصُّدُورُ joins treacherous eyes to what chests conceal, naming the gap between outward display and hidden motive under divine knowledge.
The verse describes a person's speech as pleasing to the listener, while its context calls him a fierce opponent; it directs attention from an attractive public surface to character.
The continuation shows what that speaker does after turning away: he strives to spread corruption and destroy crops and offspring, supplying conduct beneath the pleasing speech in 2:204.
وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ repeats the section's specific accusation that the person does not urge feeding the needy.
The verse says they do not honor the orphan, a direct social counterpart to 107's figure who pushes the orphan.
It adds that they do not encourage feeding the poor, closely matching the section's account of an absent exhortation.
The command not to oppress an orphan directly reverses the section's image of a hand pushing one away.
The command not to repel the asker reverses refusal of attention and aid to those in need.
Feeding the needy, orphan, and captive is the explicit positive reversal of not urging food for the poor.
The feeders seek Allah's face and neither repayment nor thanks, reversing prayer and action performed for human notice.
The next ayah says they fear a day from their Lord, completing the motive behind the God-directed feeding described in 76:8-9.
This person gives wealth to purify himself, a concrete opposite to outward devotion that serves an audience.
The giver has no favor owed by anyone to repay, the opposite of acting for a human return.
The act seeks only the face of the Most High Lord, naming the opposite audience from people who are shown a deed.
Feeding in a day of hunger reverses the failure to urge food for the needy.
The recipient is an orphan of near kin, reversing the section's mistreatment of an orphan.
The passage completes its list with a needy person in misery, the counterpart to withheld aid.
The gardeners explicitly bar a poor person from entering; their deliberate exclusion makes visible the refusal of food and help that the section diagnoses.
In their own account of punishment they say they were not among those who prayed, a direct counterpart to the section's prayer scene.
They also say they did not feed the poor, repeating the section's specific ethical failure.
They say they denied the Day of Recompense, linking the social and prayer failures in this passage to 107's opening description of denying الدين.
One command joins worship of Allah with kindness to orphans and the needy, then condemns the arrogant boaster مُخْتَالًا فَخُورًا; it gathers the section's ethical and display concerns.
The verse denies that facing east or west alone is righteousness and instead names care for orphans and the poor alongside prayer, reversing outward form without substance.
The needy do not ask persistently, so an ignorant observer thinks them self-sufficient; the verse urges giving and says Allah knows it, exposing need that a human glance misses.
The verse links coming to prayer lazily with spending only reluctantly, a specific pairing of performed worship and withheld provision like the section's prayer and ma'un.
Condemning stinginess and concealing Allah's bounty reverses the section's small, hidden withholding of help.
Do not drive away those who call on their Lord seeking His face: this directly reverses rejection of the vulnerable and redirects attention to devotion.
The command not to let one's eyes pass beyond those seeking the Lord's face, for worldly adornment, reverses the section's gaze toward social display.
The rebuke عَبَسَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ opens a scene where attention turns away from a vulnerable seeker toward a prominent man, dramatizing whom the observer chooses to see.
The next ayah identifies the entrant as blind, making the neglected person's vulnerability explicit.
Allah asks whether the blind seeker might attain purity, showing why his inner response matters more than his status.
The continuation asks whether he might receive a reminder that benefits him, completing the reason to attend to the seeker.
As for the self-sufficient man, the passage changes its description of the person receiving attention, a specific contrast with the seeker who fears and hopes to grow.
The Prophet attends to that self-sufficient man, making the misdirected human gaze explicit in the scene.
The verse says the Prophet is not responsible if the self-sufficient man fails to purify himself, clarifying why that audience should not displace the seeker.
The passage returns to the one who came striving, restoring attention to the vulnerable person previously overlooked.
The seeker fears Allah, an inward state invisible in status or appearance but decisive in this scene.
The final contrast says attention is diverted from that God-fearing seeker, making this an especially close parallel to the section's two audiences.
The righteous sleep little at night, a devotional act done beyond the public audience that the section's show-offs seek.
At dawn they ask forgiveness, continuing the private devotion that frames their material care in the next ayah.
A known right in wealth for the asker and deprived reverses the refusal of even small assistance.
These people are constant in prayer, unlike the section's people whose prayer is inattentive and governed by display.
A known share for the asker in one's wealth reverses withholding aid.
The share extends to the deprived, completing the reversal of neglected need.
The passage later says they guard their prayers, completing its picture of sustained worship rather than prayer for an audience.
This passage joins prayer, spending secretly and openly, and seeking the face of their Lord, directly contrasting the section's people-facing worship and withheld help.
The verse joins reciting Allah's book, establishing prayer, and spending secretly and publicly while hoping for a trade that will not perish, the opposite of empty display.
The preceding ayah says this same figure did not believe in Allah the Great; it completes the adjacent accusation of not urging food in 69:34.
After the orphan and poor accusations, this ayah says they devour inheritance greedily, extending the same passage's account of material harm to the vulnerable.
The passage names their intense love of wealth after describing neglect of orphan and poor, supplying a motive for withholding.
The gardeners whisper to one another as they approach their field; the next ayah reveals their concealed plan to exclude the poor.
After the display-spending verse, this asks what would prevent belief and spending from Allah's provision, then says Allah knows them; it shifts the audience from people to God.
Sincerity to Allah after repentance is the explicit reversal of a public religious act whose motive is human sight.
This verse describes spending without following it with reminders or harm, a concrete standard for giving that serves the recipient rather than the giver's display.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, so a visible gift cannot excuse harmful treatment of its recipient.
The verse says public charity is good but concealed charity given to the poor is better; it clarifies that the issue is motive and audience, not mere visibility.
People who spend secretly and publicly both receive reward from their Lord; this marks the boundary between public giving and giving for show.
Sincere worship, prayer, and zakah are the stated opposite of acting religiously for people's eyes.
Prayer is said to restrain indecency and wrongdoing; set beside 107's praying people who neglect the orphan and poor, it makes ethical effect a test of the visible act.
The thirsty person mistakes a mirage for water but finds nothing on reaching it; this separate visual image parallels the section's mirror that shows an image without depth.
The verse reverses visual agency: human eyes do not encompass Allah, while He encompasses eyes; its context concerns divine incomparability, sharpening who sees without claiming people see God.
It says eyes are not blind, but hearts within chests are blind تَعْمَى الْقُلُوبُ الَّتِي فِي الصُّدُورِ, naming the difference between eyesight and inward insight in the source's root gloss.
The human is described as بصيرة against himself even while offering excuses, shifting the decisive witness inward from the audience he presents himself to.
Do not turn your cheek contemptuously toward people or walk exultantly: this addresses the public face and bearing that the source's secondary dictionary sense calls displayed demeanor.
أَرَأَيْتَ asks the listener to consider one who takes desire as a god, then describes sight and heart as covered; it echoes the section's call to see a person's ruling inner orientation.
This parallel أَفَرَأَيْتَ passage again names one who takes desire as a god and says hearing, heart, and sight are sealed, making inward perception the issue.
The verse condemns people who want praise for what they have not done, a specific gap between public acclaim and actual deed like the section's display.
The hypocrites publicly testify to the Messenger, while the same ayah declares them liars; this makes the displayed statement diverge from inward truth.
They use oaths as a shield and turn people from Allah's way, extending the prior verse's false public testimony into action.
The passage says they believed then disbelieved and their hearts were sealed, specifying the concealed state behind the outward presentation.
The mosque-builders swear they intended only good, while Allah declares them liars; a public religious setting masks a contrary purpose, close to prayer staged for observers.
